question: Do debate, market-making and recursive reward modeling work in sandwiching trials?
asked_by: Bowman et al., Measuring Progress on Scalable Oversight for Large Language Models
remaining_question: In a sandwiching trial with non-expert humans, a model stronger than them, and expert or ground-truth scoring, do multi-turn debate between model debaters, market making, and genuinely recursive reward modeling (assistant models trained in earlier rounds helping the non-experts evaluate the next model) raise non-expert accuracy above consultancy and above simple deference to the model?

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2311.08702v1: Debate Helps Supervise Unreliable Experts
findings.claim: Michael et al. call their study a variant of the sandwiching design that Bowman et al. (2022) implement, with human debaters standing in as the experts. On hard reading-comprehension questions, non-expert judges who never see the passage reach 84% accuracy with debate versus 74% with consultancy, where one expert argues for an answer that is correct half of the time.
findings.setting: Human-subject experiment. Expert human debaters (with some comparisons to AI debaters) have access to the passage; the non-expert human judge has not read it and sees only the experts' arguments and short quotes the debaters selectively reveal. Hard reading-comprehension questions; one debater argues for the correct answer and the other for an incorrect answer. The baseline is consultancy, where a single expert argues for one answer that is correct half of the time. The authors call the design a variant of Bowman et al.'s sandwiching design whose difference is that human debaters serve as the experts, as a proxy for future powerful AI systems, rather than a model.
findings.bears_on: The debate part of the question in a human sandwiching variant. This is an atlas paper: its CORE record is already in the checked answer. The XREF record that names the design as sandwiching is listed under atlas_records_missed.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2507.19486v1: Confirmation bias: A challenge for scalable oversight
findings.claim: In a paradigm similar to Bowman et al. (2022), additionally presenting participants with a one-turn debate (arguments generated by the language model defending each of the two possible answers) did not give any of the overall benefits the authors hypothesised. In an exploratory analysis, the arguments present group had an accuracy advantage specifically in the rare cases where the LLM was incorrect. In contrast to Bowman et al., LLM-assisted participants achieved poorer performance than LLMs alone.
findings.setting: Human-subject experiment: 192 participants recruited through Prolific, randomly assigned in a 2x2 factorial design: arguments present vs absent (whether participants were shown two competing arguments, one supporting each answer choice, generated by the language model), crossed with incentive awareness (whether participants were informed about a potential bonus payment). Participants answer difficult factual questions with two possible answers while interacting with a language model; the key test compares participants' accuracy after interacting with the model with the accuracy of the model alone, not with domain experts. The one-turn debate is two arguments from one language model, not an interactive debate between two models.
findings.bears_on: The debate part, in a paradigm the authors call similar to Bowman et al. (2022), with Prolific participants and a comparison against the model alone. It covers only a minimal one-turn debate (model-written arguments for each answer). Market making and RRM are not tested.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2608.17776v1: Debate Training Reduces Reward Hacking in RLAIF
findings.claim: A Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy was RL-trained against a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge on mathematics tasks where final-answer correctness is verifiable. The single-player RLAIF baseline quickly hacked the judge, while generator-critic debate maintained judge performance throughout training, leading to a higher peak validation accuracy (45% performance gap recovered) that persisted through many RL steps. Peak validation accuracy under debate was ~2 percentage points higher than baseline, recovering roughly 45% of the gap to the RLVR roofline; the authors say the absolute effect is small and that the maintained judge performance and peak accuracy are the more practically important findings. They note disanalogies with humans overseeing superhuman AI, because their judge and policy share similar architectures and training distributions.
findings.setting: Experiment: RL fine-tuning of a Gemini 2.5 Flash-class policy against a frozen, weaker Gemini 2.5 Flash Lite judge, deliberately set up as a weaker judge supervising a stronger policy to model the scalable oversight setting. Mathematics tasks; final-answer correctness is verifiable and used to measure reward hacking. A single-player RLAIF baseline is compared with debate; the performance gap recovered is stated relative to an RLVR roofline. The overseer is an LLM judge rather than non-expert humans, and correctness is checked against verifiable final answers rather than by experts.
findings.bears_on: The debate part, at the training stage, in an AI-only analogue of a sandwiching design: the weak overseer is a weaker LLM judge, not non-expert humans. Market making and RRM are not tested.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2511.17621v2: From Competition to Coordination: Market Making as a Scalable Framework for Safe and Aligned Multi-Agent LLM Systems
findings.claim: In the authors' market-making implementation, a trader model generates an argument intended to maximally shift the market maker M's prediction value, and M produces new judgments that consider the trader's previous arguments; the impact is measured by comparing the accuracy of M's final judgment with the accuracy of its initial judgment (the baseline without trader influence). They find a net increase in the percentage of accurate answers: each model family has an overall improvement in accuracy over their baselines in the majority of the datasets, excluding ETHICS Justice. Their experiments exclusively used identical models for the market maker and trader roles within each trial; they say this configuration may not capture the dynamics that emerge when models with different capabilities, training objectives, or architectures interact. There is therefore no capability gap and no weaker overseer, so market making is not tested in a sandwiching trial.
findings.setting: Experiment with prompted models: a market-maker model M and a trader, filled by identical models in every trial. The trader argues to shift M's prediction value; the cycle stops after at most N = 10 judgments or when the range of the last three prediction values is at most T = 0.2. The accuracy of M's final judgment is compared with that of its initial judgment, per model family, on several datasets including ETHICS Justice. Both roles are models, and the judgment whose accuracy is measured is M's own, not a separate weaker overseer's.
findings.bears_on: The market-making part: the only later empirical market-making implementation found besides Lang et al.'s weak-to-strong variant. It is outside the sandwiching setting.

passages.text:
Given M’s judgment, the trader model then generates an argument intended to maximally shift M’s
prediction value. This is analogous to a trader introducing new information to change the market
price.
Each subsequent iteration proceeds with M producing a new judgment while also considering the
trader’s previous arguments. Exact prompting details are provided in Appendix B. The cycle repeats
until the market maker has provided at most N judgments or has reached an equilibrium; we consider
an equilibrium to have been reached when the range of the last three prediction values satisfies
max{pt−2 , pt−1 , pt } − min{pt−2 , pt−1 , pt } ≤ T,
where T is a threshold constant. In our experiments, we set N = 10 and T = 0.2.
Finally, we measure the impact of market making by comparing the accuracy of M’s final judgment
before termination against the accuracy of its initial judgment (i.e., the baseline without trader
influence) across all dataset samples.

We find a net increase in the percentage of accurate answers provided by the models. This can be seen
in Figure 2 where each model family has an overall improvement in accuracy over their baselines in
the majority of the datasets excluding ETHICS Justice.

Our experiments exclusively employed identical models for both market maker and trader roles
within each trial. This configuration may not capture the dynamics that emerge when models with
different capabilities, training objectives, or architectures interact.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2602.04210v2: Steering LLMs via Scalable Interactive Oversight
findings.claim: The authors validate their interactive oversight method, which they describe as a recursive interaction that iteratively decodes vague user intent into expert-level specifications before execution, using what they call the "sandwich" protocol (Bowman et al., 2022): a non-expert user attempts to guide a strong model to achieve tasks that only an expert can verify. On full-stack website development, where non-experts produce Product Requirement Documents (PRDs), they report that the method significantly outperforms standard vibe coding baselines (e.g. Claude Code, Gemini CLI) and vanilla interaction methods, improving alignment scores by up to 54%. To scale the experiments, non-expert behaviour is emulated by a user simulator implemented with deepseek-R1, and large-scale evaluation uses an LLM judge based on Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct. In 10 cases, one hired non-expert collaborated with GPT-5, and alignment scores increased as interaction rounds progressed.
findings.setting: Mostly simulated sandwich-protocol evaluation of an interactive steering method: a non-expert, emulated by a deepseek-R1 user simulator when experiments are scaled, guides a strong model to produce PRDs for full-stack website development; large-scale evaluation is by an LLM judge based on Qwen3-235B-A22B-Instruct rather than by human experts; plus a 10-case study in which one hired non-expert collaborates with GPT-5. The method steers the model through interaction before execution; it is not debate, market making or recursive reward modeling.
findings.bears_on: The RRM part, loosely: the closest recursive protocol found (the authors call it a recursive interaction) that is tested in a self-described sandwich set-up, mostly with a simulated non-expert and an LLM judge. It is not recursive reward modeling.

findings.later_paper: arXiv 2406.04604v4: Learning Task Decomposition to Assist Humans in Competitive Programming
findings.claim: In a human study on competitive programming, assistance from the authors' decomposition model let non-expert programmers repair model-generated programs about as well and as efficiently as unassisted experts. Strict accuracy of repaired programs rose from 30.0% to 63.3% for non-experts and from 56.7% to 90% for experts (paired t-tests, p < 0.01). The authors note that their non-experts are still more skilled than novice programmers.
findings.setting: Human-subject experiment: expert and non-expert programmers repair model-generated programs with or without the authors' decomposition model; strict accuracy of repaired programs and labeling efficiency are measured. The non-experts could solve 30% of the problems and are still more skilled than novice programmers. Decomposition assistance, not debate, market making or recursive reward modeling.
findings.bears_on: The RRM part only by analogy: a sandwiching-like expert/non-expert comparison for one level of AI decomposition assistance. It is not recursive reward modeling.

Decomposition enables non-experts to be comparable with experts Remarkably, when assisted
with our decomposition model, non-experts achieve

Humans provide higher-quality labels with decomposition Beyond efficiency, we evaluate how
decomposition impacts the final quality of human
labels. As shown in Figure 3, our decomposition model enables humans to repair more modelgenerated programs. For instance, decomposition
improves the strict accuracy of repaired programs
from 56.7% to 90% for experts and from 30.0%
to 63.3% for non-experts. Paired t-tests confirm
the significance (p < 0.01) of these improvements.

One limitation of our work is that our non-expert
participants, who could solve 30% of the problems while spending 74 minutes, are still more
skilled than novice programmers (e.g., programmers who can only solve Leetcode easy-level
problems) or non-programmers. Nonetheless, we
demonstrate the effectiveness of our decomposition model, which successfully enables assisted
non-experts to be comparable with non-assisted experts. We leave the investigation of leveraging decomposition to assist novice programmers or even
non-programmers as future work.
